hints: Speed = distance ÷ time.
solution: $v = \dfrac{d}{t} = \dfrac{100}{20} = 5$ m/s

prompt: Match each quantity to its SI unit.
hints: Acceleration is a change in velocity (m/s) every second.
solution: Speed → m/s; acceleration → m/s²; distance → m; time → s.

prompt: Velocity is speed in a particular [[a]]. Acceleration is the rate of change of [[b]].
hints: "15 m/s north" is a velocity. What extra information does it have compared with a speed?
solution: Velocity is speed in a particular **direction**. Acceleration is the rate of change of **velocity**: how much the velocity changes each second.

prompt: Which of these is an **instantaneous** speed?

options.text: A car's speedometer reads 80 km/h as it passes a sign
A family drives 240 km in 3 hours
A runner finishes a 5 km race in 25 minutes
A ferry takes 3 hours to cross 90 km of sea

feedback.b: Total distance ÷ total time gives an average speed for the whole trip.
feedback.c: This gives the runner's average speed over the whole race.
feedback.d: This gives the ferry's average speed for the crossing.

hints: Instantaneous means "at one instant" (one moment).
solution: The speedometer reading is the speed **at that moment**, so it is instantaneous. The others give average speeds (total distance ÷ total time).

prompt: How long does it take Sione to run 400 m at an average speed of 5 m/s?
hints: Rearrange speed = distance ÷ time to make time the subject.
solution: $t = \dfrac{d}{v} = \dfrac{400}{5} = 80$ s

prompt: What is the name of the quantity that tells you how quickly an object's velocity changes?
hints: Its unit is m/s².
solution: **Acceleration**: $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{t}$, measured in m/s².

modelAnswer: The line from 0 s to 4 s is steeper than the line from 12 s to 20 s. At the start, her speed changed by 8 m/s in 4 s, so her acceleration was 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m/s². At the end, her speed changed by 8 m/s in 8 s, so she slowed down at 8 ÷ 8 = 1 m/s² (an acceleration of −1 m/s²). Her speed changed twice as quickly at the start.

rubric.criterion: States that the line is steeper at the start than at the end (the same change in speed happens in less time)
Correct calculations: 2 m/s² at the start and 1 m/s² (or −1 m/s²) at the end

hints: Compare the steepness of the two sloping parts of the line.
Work out the acceleration for each part: change in speed ÷ time.
solution: On a speed–time graph, the steepness (gradient) is the acceleration. Start: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m/s². End: 8 ÷ 8 = 1 m/s² of slowing down. The steeper start means she sped up faster than she slowed down.

stem: A ferry crosses Cook Strait from Wellington to Picton. The trip is about 92 km and takes 3 hours 30 minutes.
prompt: What is the ferry's average speed for the trip, in km/h? Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
hints: Write 3 hours 30 minutes as a decimal number of hours.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
solution: 3 h 30 min = 3.5 h (not 3.3 h, because 30 minutes is half an hour). $v = \dfrac{92}{3.5} = 26.28...$, so about **26.3 km/h**.

stem: A ferry crosses Cook Strait from Wellington to Picton. The trip is about 92 km and takes 3 hours 30 minutes.
prompt: As it leaves Wellington, the ferry speeds up from rest to 6 m/s in 2 minutes. What is its average acceleration?
hints: Change the time into seconds first.
Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time taken.
solution: 2 minutes = 120 s. $a = \dfrac{6 - 0}{120} =$ **0.05 m/s²**: a very small acceleration, which is why a big ferry takes a long time to get up to speed.

stem: A ferry crosses Cook Strait from Wellington to Picton. The trip is about 92 km and takes 3 hours 30 minutes.
prompt: Two ferries pass each other in the middle of Cook Strait. One is heading north at 25 km/h and the other is heading south at 25 km/h. Do they have the same speed? Do they have the same velocity? Explain your answers.
modelAnswer: They have the same speed, 25 km/h, because speed only tells you how fast something is going. They have different velocities, because velocity is speed in a particular direction: one ferry has a velocity of 25 km/h north and the other 25 km/h south.

rubric.criterion: Same speed (25 km/h), because speed is just how fast they are going
Different velocities, because velocity includes direction and they are going in opposite directions

hints: What extra information does a velocity include that a speed doesn't?
solution: Speed = how fast. Velocity = how fast **and** in which direction. Same speed, opposite directions, so different velocities.

prompt: Which formula is used to calculate speed?

feedback.b: This is upside down. Speed is how much distance is covered in each unit of time.
feedback.c: Going the same distance in more time means a **lower** speed, so you divide by the time, not multiply.
feedback.d: You can't subtract a time from a distance. They are different kinds of quantity.

hints: A speed in m/s tells you the number of metres travelled each second.
solution: $\text{speed} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$. The unit m/s (metres **per** second) reminds you: metres divided by seconds.

prompt: What do we call speed in a particular direction, such as 15 m/s north?
hints: This quantity changes when a car turns a corner, even if its speed stays the same.
solution: **Velocity** is speed in a given direction. 15 m/s north and 15 m/s south are the same speed, but different velocities.

prompt: On a distance–time graph, a horizontal line means the object is [[a]]. On a speed–time graph, a horizontal line means the object is moving at a [[b]] speed.
hints: On a distance–time graph, a flat line means the distance is not changing.
On a speed–time graph, a flat line means the speed is not changing.
solution: Flat distance–time line: the distance isn't changing, so the object is **stationary**. Flat speed–time line: the speed isn't changing, so it is moving at a **constant** speed. Always read the axis labels first!

prompt: A netball pass travels 12 m in 0.8 s. What is the ball's average speed?

feedback.b: That is 12 × 0.8. Speed is distance **divided by** time.
feedback.c: That is 0.8 ÷ 12. The division is upside down.
feedback.d: That is 12 − 0.8. You need to divide the distance by the time.

hints: Use speed = distance ÷ time.
solution: $v = \dfrac{d}{t} = \dfrac{12}{0.8} =$ **15 m/s**. Dividing by a number less than 1 gives a bigger answer.

prompt: What does the **steepness** (gradient) of the line on a distance–time graph tell you?

feedback.b: It is the gradient of a **speed–time** graph that gives acceleration.
feedback.c: The total distance is read from the vertical axis at the end of the journey, not from the steepness.
feedback.d: The time is read from the horizontal axis.

hints: Steepness = how much the distance changes for each second.
solution: Gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time = **speed**. A steeper line means a faster speed, and a flat line means the object has stopped.

prompt: Match each graph shape to the motion it shows.

Speed–time graph: a straight line sloping upwards
Speed–time graph: a straight line sloping downwards

hints: Check the axis label first: is it distance or speed going up the side?
solution: Distance–time: flat = stationary; straight upward slope = constant speed. Speed–time: upward slope = speeding up; downward slope = slowing down.

prompt: Which of these is a **velocity**, not just a speed?

feedback.b: This only says how fast. A velocity also needs a direction.
feedback.c: 'On the motorway' is a place, not a direction.
feedback.d: This gives a distance and a time (a speed of 8 m/s), but no direction.

hints: A velocity has a size **and** a direction.
solution: Velocity = speed + direction. Only **20 m/s towards the north** includes a direction.

prompt: Wiremu jogs at a steady 3 m/s for 2 minutes. How far does he jog?

feedback.b: That is 3 × 2, but the 2 is in minutes. Change the time to seconds first (2 min = 120 s).
feedback.c: That is 3 ÷ 2. Distance = speed × time, and the time must be in seconds.
feedback.d: That is 120 ÷ 3. Dividing the time by the speed doesn't give a distance.

hints: Use distance = speed × time.
The speed is in metres per **second**, so the time must be in seconds.

prompt: A bungy jumper leaps off a bridge near Queenstown. Starting from rest, she is falling at 15 m/s after 1.5 s, before the cord starts to stretch. What is her average acceleration?
hints: Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time taken.
'From rest' means her starting velocity is 0 m/s.
solution: $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{t} = \dfrac{15 - 0}{1.5} =$ **10 m/s²**. This is the acceleration caused by gravity when air resistance is small.

prompt: A car has an acceleration of 3 m/s². What does this mean?

options.text: Its velocity increases by 3 m/s every second
It is moving at a steady 3 m/s
It takes 3 s to reach its top speed

feedback.b: Travelling 3 m every second is a **speed** of 3 m/s, not an acceleration.
feedback.c: A steady speed (in a straight line) means zero acceleration.
feedback.d: Acceleration tells you how quickly the velocity changes, not how long it takes to reach top speed.

hints: The unit m/s² can be read as '(m/s) per second'.
solution: 3 m/s² means the velocity goes up by **3 m/s every second**: for example 0, 3, 6 and 9 m/s after 0, 1, 2 and 3 seconds.

prompt: A car drives around a roundabout at a constant 30 km/h. Explain why the car is accelerating, even though its speed is not changing.
modelAnswer: Velocity is speed in a particular direction. As the car goes around the roundabout its direction keeps changing, so its velocity keeps changing, even though its speed stays at 30 km/h. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so a changing velocity means the car is accelerating.

rubric.criterion: Velocity includes direction (velocity is speed in a particular direction)
The car's direction is changing, so its velocity is changing
Acceleration is a change in velocity, so the car is accelerating

hints: What is the difference between speed and velocity?
What is acceleration a change in?
solution: Acceleration means a change in **velocity**, and velocity includes direction. Turning changes the direction, so the car accelerates even at a steady speed.

prompt: A car is travelling at 90 km/h. The driver looks down at a phone for 4 s. How far does the car travel in that time?
hints: Change 90 km/h into m/s first.
Then use distance = speed × time.
solution: $90 \div 3.6 = 25$ m/s. $d = vt = 25 \times 4 =$ **100 m**: about the length of a rugby field, travelled without looking at the road.

prompt: Select **all** the objects that have **zero acceleration**.

options.text: A bike leaning against the school fence
A skydiver falling straight down at a steady terminal velocity
An object whose distance–time graph is a straight, sloping line
An object whose speed–time graph is a horizontal line
A netball slowing down as it rolls across the court
A car going round a corner at a steady 50 km/h
An object whose speed–time graph is a straight line sloping upwards

hints: Zero acceleration means the velocity (speed **and** direction) is not changing.
solution: Zero acceleration means a constant velocity: not moving at all (the bike), or moving at a steady speed in a straight line (the skydiver at terminal velocity, a straight sloping distance–time line, a flat speed–time line). The netball is slowing down, the car turning a corner is changing direction, and an upward-sloping speed–time line means speeding up, so these are all accelerating.

prompt: Hana walks 1.2 km to school at 1.5 m/s. Her brother leaves home 5 minutes after her and cycles the same route at 5 m/s. How many seconds before Hana does her brother arrive at school?
hints: Change 1.2 km into metres and 5 minutes into seconds.
Work out when each of them arrives, measured from the moment Hana leaves home.
solution: Hana: $t = \dfrac{1200}{1.5} = 800$ s. Brother: $t = \dfrac{1200}{5} = 240$ s, but he starts 300 s later, so he arrives $300 + 240 = 540$ s after Hana left. He arrives $800 - 540 =$ **260 s** before her (4 minutes 20 seconds).

prompt: Tama cycles 6 km to the beach at an average speed of 12 km/h. He is tired on the way home, so he cycles the same 6 km back at 6 km/h. What is his average speed for the whole trip?

feedback.b: 9 km/h is the average of the two speeds, but he spent longer going slowly, so you can't just average them. Use total distance ÷ total time.
feedback.c: That adds the two speeds together. Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
feedback.d: That was only his speed on the way home.

hints: Work out how long each half of the trip took.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
solution: There: $6 \div 12 = 0.5$ h. Back: $6 \div 6 = 1$ h. Total: 12 km in 1.5 h, so the average speed is $12 \div 1.5 =$ **8 km/h**. It is less than 9 km/h because he spent more time at the slower speed.

prompt: Some roads have **average speed cameras**. One camera records the time a car passes it, and a second camera 10 km further along the road does the same. A car takes 5 minutes to travel between the two cameras. The speed limit is 100 km/h. The driver says, "My speedometer read 95 km/h at both cameras, so I didn't speed." Explain whether the driver broke the speed limit.
modelAnswer: The car's average speed between the cameras was 10 km ÷ 5 min = 2 km per minute, which is 2 × 60 = 120 km/h. The speedometer readings of 95 km/h are instantaneous speeds: they only show the speed at the moment the car passed each camera, not in between. For the average to be 120 km/h, the car must have been travelling faster than 100 km/h for at least part of the time between the cameras. So the driver did break the speed limit.

rubric.criterion: Correct average speed: 10 km in 5 min = 120 km/h (or 2 km per minute, or about 33 m/s)
Explains that 95 km/h at each camera is an instantaneous speed, which doesn't tell you the speed between the cameras
Concludes that the average is above 100 km/h, so the car must have gone faster than 100 km/h for some of the time and broke the limit

hints: Work out the car's average speed between the cameras, in km/h.
How could the average be higher than the speed at both cameras?
solution: 5 min = $\dfrac{5}{60}$ h, so the average speed is $10 \div \dfrac{5}{60} = 120$ km/h. An average of 120 km/h is impossible unless the car went over 100 km/h at some point, so the driver broke the limit.
